s: Your project's governance plan requires steering committee approval for scope changes. The committee has not met for six weeks because two members are travelling, and a customer-requested change needs a decision within a week. What should you do?
o: Get verbal agreement from the available members and proceed on their word alone
Pass the decision to the customer's executive sponsor so it is not delayed
Ask the governance chair to invoke a delegate or an out-of-cycle written vote
Tell the customer to wait and re-plan around the next scheduled meeting date
e: Governance decision rights are not bypassed, but good governance plans define alternates. Use the plan's own interim path or ask the chair to invoke one. Informal verbal agreement, going around the committee and simply waiting all fail the control or the deadline.

s: The steering committee asks you to report only green status to a regulator-facing dashboard while the project is actually amber on schedule. What is the BEST response?
o: Show green on the dashboard but brief the regulator verbally on the schedule slip
Report green now and correct it next period if the schedule does not recover
Report amber only in internal documents, leaving the regulator dashboard as requested
Report accurate amber status with the recovery plan and raise it through governance
e: Honesty and responsibility under PMI's code take precedence. Raise the concern through governance rather than comply with misleading reporting.

s: Midway through delivery, a new data-protection rule makes one planned feature non-compliant in a market that accounts for 20% of expected revenue. The feature is already 60% built. What should you do FIRST?
o: Pause the feature and ask legal to confirm the rule applies before any further work is done
Assess the compliance impact and options, then take a decision through change control
Finish the remaining 40% as planned and add a compliance patch after release
Withdraw the affected market from scope and update the business case accordingly
e: Compliance is a constraint, but the response is an assessed trade-off decided by the right authority. Stopping or continuing blindly are both premature.

s: A change request is approved. Two weeks later you realise the approved cost impact was calculated using the old resource rate. What is the BEST action?
o: Reassess the corrected impact, resubmit it to the CCB and update the baselines
Record the rate error in the change log and cover the gap from contingency reserve
Notify the sponsor informally and let the approved baseline stand as it is
Withdraw the approval and ask the requester to raise a fresh change from scratch
e: The approval was based on wrong data. Transparency and the change process require resubmission.

s: A recurring impediment is slowing the team: a shared test environment is booked by another team for two days each week. The functional manager of that team will not release it. What do you do?
o: Ask the team to reschedule their testing around the booked days and track the delay
Request budget for a second test environment so the team no longer shares one
Raise it at the next retrospective and let the team find a workaround themselves
Log the issue, quantify its impact and escalate it to a decision maker who can arbitrate
e: Impediments outside your authority are logged, quantified and escalated with impact data.

s: A risk was assessed at 10% probability and had no response planned. It now occurs. What should the project manager do FIRST?
o: Record it as a lesson learned, revise the probability upward and move on with the plan
Request management reserve at once to fund a full recovery response
Treat it as an issue: assess impact, apply a workaround and update the logs
Report it to the steering committee and hold work until they decide
e: A risk that occurs becomes an issue. Unplanned responses are workarounds. Management reserve is drawn only with approval.

s: Two risks have equal expected monetary value, but one is a $2M loss at 5% and the other a $100K loss at 100%. The sponsor is highly risk-averse. How should you prioritise?
o: Address the certain risk first, since a guaranteed loss outranks a possible one
Treat them as equal priority because the expected monetary values match
Address the severe, unlikely risk first because the sponsor is risk-averse
Accept both and cover them from a single shared contingency reserve
e: EMV ignores risk appetite. A risk-averse sponsor weights severe impact more heavily.

s: A hybrid project's agile team adopts a new technical approach inside an iteration that affects an interface promised to another team in the predictive part. What is the BEST action?
o: Proceed inside the iteration, since the agile team owns its own backlog and approach
Raise a change against the integration baseline and agree the impact with the other team
Ask the predictive team to adapt its side and confirm after the iteration ends
Hold the new approach until final integration testing and then reconcile the interface
e: In hybrid delivery, interface commitments are controlled across approaches. Coordinate through the agreed governance.

s: A competitor announces a feature that makes part of your project's planned value obsolete. The project is on schedule. What should you do?
o: Assess the impact on the business case and bring options to the sponsor
Keep to the approved plan, since the project is still on schedule
Add an equivalent feature to scope straight away to match the competitor
Pause delivery spend until the market settles, then reassess later in the year
e: External changes must be evaluated against value. The decision belongs to the sponsor and governance.

s: The project will change how 200 staff do their daily work. Training is planned but resistance is building. What would BEST support the organisational change?
o: Extend the training programme with extra hours and refresher sessions for all 200 staff
Postpone go-live until resistance has settled, then resume the planned rollout
Engage impacted groups early, use champions and align leaders on benefits
Have leadership mandate use of the new process through a formal policy notice
e: Organisational change depends on engagement, sponsorship and champions, not only training or mandate.

s: At the end of each iteration the team finds the same integration problem. What is the BEST way to drive continuous improvement?
o: Agree an experiment at the retrospective with an owner and check the result next time
Record the problem as a lesson learned and review it with the sponsor at project close
Add an integration phase at the end of the release to catch such problems
Assign one person to monitor integration and report issues to the manager each week
e: Continuous improvement uses small experiments with owners and checks, not deferred lessons.

s: A project manager in a matrix organisation realises that two functional managers have conflicting priorities for the same resource and no governance group exists to arbitrate. What should you do?
o: Escalate to the common sponsor or portfolio owner and propose a decision forum
Allocate the resource to whichever manager has the more senior position
Bring in contractors to cover both managers' demands and log the extra cost as a risk
Pause the project until the two managers settle their priorities themselves
e: Governance defines who decides. When it is missing, establish or escalate to the authority that can decide.

s: Two team members from different cultures keep misreading each other's direct and indirect communication styles. The work is slipping. What is the BEST approach?
o: Refer the matter to HR to coach both people on cross-cultural communication
Facilitate a talk on communication styles and agree working norms
Move one of them to a different workstream so they stop interacting
Ask both to follow the project manager's communication style for all exchanges
e: Build shared norms and cultural awareness. Separation or escalation skips the simplest fix.

s: A stakeholder you have classified as high power, low interest begins publicly criticising the project on social media. What is the BEST action?
o: Publish a factual rebuttal of the criticism on the project's own channels
Take no action, since low interest means the comments will probably fade soon
Meet them privately to understand the concern and adjust the engagement plan
Ask the sponsor to tell the stakeholder to stop commenting on the project
e: Engage directly to understand and resolve the concern. Suppression or public rebuttal escalates the problem.

s: A critical team member will leave in two weeks and holds undocumented knowledge. What is the MOST effective way to help ensure knowledge transfer?
o: Bring in an outside consultant to rebuild the knowledge after the person leaves
Ask them to write a detailed handover document during their final week
Log the departure as a risk and accept it, since two weeks is too short
Start now with pairing, recorded walkthroughs and a successor handover
e: Knowledge transfer works best through active pairing and walkthroughs planned early, not a late document.

s: The communications management plan says weekly status email, but stakeholders say they never read it. What should you do?
o: Move to a twice-weekly email so the status is harder for people to miss
Ask stakeholders how they want to receive information and update the plan
Keep the weekly email as planned, since the stakeholders approved the plan
Replace the weekly email with a monthly summary to reduce reader fatigue
e: Communication is effective only when received. Update the plan from stakeholder feedback.

s: A self-organising team makes a decision you believe is wrong but which is within their authority and not a risk to compliance. What do you do?
o: Share your concern and data, let the team decide and review the result
Take the issue to the sponsor and ask for a ruling on the team's decision
Overrule the decision and direct the team to the approach you prefer
Say nothing and let the team learn from the outcome without any input
e: A servant leader informs but respects the team's decision rights, then learns from the result.

s: Team members describe the project goal in three different ways. What should you do?
o: Circulate the charter and ask each member to restate the goal in writing
Choose the clearest of the three versions and publish it as the project goal
Facilitate a session to build a shared vision linked to the business case
Let the descriptions stand, as long as everyone delivers their own tasks on time
e: A common vision is built with the team and tied to the value the project delivers.

s: A stakeholder expects a feature to be delivered at no extra cost, but it is not in the agreed scope. What is the BEST step?
o: Decline the request and point to the signed scope without further discussion
Have the team fit it in within existing capacity without raising a cost
Deliver it as a goodwill gesture and recover the cost on a later change
Clarify the scope, explore the need and process it as a change if justified
e: Align expectations by clarifying scope and the need, then use change control.

s: CPI is 0.80. The sponsor confirms the overspend came from a one-time supplier problem that is now resolved, and the remaining work will be done at the budgeted rate. Which EAC formula is MOST appropriate?
o: BAC − EV
AC + (BAC − EV) / (CPI × SPI)
BAC / CPI
AC + (BAC − EV)
e: When variance is atypical and future work proceeds at the budgeted rate, use EAC = AC + (BAC − EV). BAC / CPI assumes the inefficiency continues.

s: Activity D has a duration of 6 days, an early start of day 10 and a late finish of day 20. What is its total float?
o: 0 days
4 days
6 days
10 days
e: Early finish = 16. Float = late finish − early finish = 20 − 16 = 4 days.

s: A fixed-price contract has a scope that the seller says is incomplete. The seller wants more money. The buyer's requirements document was unclear. What should you do?
o: Reject the claim outright, since a fixed price puts all scope risk on the seller
Offer a partial payment now and settle the rest of the dispute in final negotiations
Review with procurement and legal and issue a change order if the increase is justified
Terminate for default and re-tender the work with a clearer scope statement
e: Unclear buyer requirements may justify a change. Follow the contract and use a formal change order.

s: A requirement in the traceability matrix has no linked test case. What should you do?
o: Mark it verified on the basis of the developer's demonstration of the feature
Add a test for it or confirm through change control that it is no longer needed
Remove the row from the matrix so the traceability record stays complete
Leave the gap and note it in the register, as the matrix is a guide and not a gate
e: Traceability exposes verification gaps. Close the gap with a test, or remove the requirement through change control, never quietly.

s: Defects found by customers are rising while internal testing shows few. What is the BEST first action?
o: Analyse the cause by comparing test coverage with customer usage and close the gap
Add more testers to the internal test cycle to raise the number of defects found
Extend the warranty period so customers feel covered while defects are fixed
Ask support to triage incoming customer defect reports and cap how many reach the team
e: Find the root cause (a coverage gap) before adding effort.

s: A team's burn-up chart shows scope rising at the same rate as work completed, so the finish line never gets closer. What is the BEST response?
o: Ask the team to raise its velocity so the work catches up with the scope
Extend the release date to absorb the added scope and keep all items
Freeze the backlog and refuse any new items without consulting the product owner
Take it to the product owner to prioritise and agree what is out of the release
e: Rising scope shown on a burn-up is a prioritisation conversation with the product owner.

s: The customer will not sign off at closure because the support team has not been trained. What should you do?
o: Check whether training is in scope and agree a path to acceptance with the customer
Ask the sponsor to sign off on the customer's behalf so closure can proceed
Close the project on the delivery date and record the training gap as a follow-up
Archive the project records and hand the training issue over to the support team lead
e: Closure needs acceptance and transition. Confirm scope and agree a path to acceptance.

s: An item on the backlog has a high effort and low value. The team enjoys working on it. What should the PM encourage?
o: Re-rank with the product owner by value and do the highest-value items first
Let the team finish the item, since motivation drives the quality of delivery
Remove all low-value items from the backlog to keep it short and focused
Outsource the item to a contractor so the team can move on to other work
e: Value-based delivery prioritises business value over team preference.

s: The project is under budget but the sponsor wants to reallocate the unspent money to another project. Funds were approved for this project's cost baseline. What do you do?
o: Refuse the request, since the funds were approved for this project only
Move the funds yourself and record it as a forecast adjustment next month
Release the funds to the sponsor once the team confirms no further spend is needed
Request the reallocation through governance and funding procedures
e: Reallocating approved funds is a governance decision, not a PM discretion.
